paragraphs: For two and a half months, from mid-February to the end of April 2025, I studied abroad at the Medical University of Vienna and did clinical clerkships at the Vienna General Hospital (AKH Wien). At every stage, the preparation for applying to study abroad, the procedures and preparation for study abroad after the destination was decided, and the actual study abroad, there was much to learn and it was an irreplaceable experience.

First, in pediatrics, I did my clerkship for the first two weeks in pediatric cardiology and for the latter two weeks in pediatric nephrology, gastroenterology and rheumatology. In pediatric cardiology, congenital heart disease was especially common, and I could see a wide range of patients, from severe cases and diseases I had never seen in Japanese hospitals to cases indicated for heart transplantation. What stayed in my memory was being able to listen to heart murmurs. The supervising doctors were also kind, and when I went to examine a patient, took findings and stated what I thought, I could receive feedback. They also gave easy-to-understand lectures on how to read ECGs. In pediatric nephrology I observed dialysis and abdominal ultrasound. Ultrasound cannot be performed well if the patient moves. But children often move or cry during ultrasound, so some doctors set up all sorts of devices in the ultrasound room in order to perform the examination properly. In pediatric gastroenterology and rheumatology I was allowed to see referral consultations, outpatient clinics following the course of chronic diseases, and liver biopsies.

Next I did my clerkship in radiology, where division of labor was advanced, with a chest X-ray group, CT group, MRI group, interventional therapy group, trauma group, ultrasound group and breast surgery group (handling both mammography and biopsy). After being taught the doctors' methods of image reading, I actually tried reading myself and had my answers checked, which was very instructive. Many young doctors were also active, and I often heard stories about their high quality of life.

I rotated through obstetrics and gynecology for one week each, and was able to observe and assist in operations for rare cases and also observe very subdivided outpatient clinics. For example, the obstetrics outpatient clinics were divided into multiple pregnancy clinic, maternal risk clinic, fetal risk clinic and so on, which was very interesting.

Finally I did my clerkship in general surgery, which, like the other departments, handles a wide variety of cases, and I was able to learn about many kinds of cases. General surgery was the only place among my clerkships where I could do the clerkship together with exchange students from other countries. Even within Europe, Austria is very popular, and there were many students doing clerkships aiming to work in Austria in the future and many doctors who visit Vienna's hospitals even after becoming doctors.

Many people in Austria speak English, and especially with healthcare workers, I could often converse in English with whomever I spoke to, so I did not struggle on the language side as much as I had imagined, but still, living surrounded by an unfamiliar language (German) was sometimes stressful at first. From partway through, I noticed that preparing to say even one German phrase makes a slightly good impression, and I found doctors who would explain and interpret in English, and gradually got used to life in a non-English-speaking country.

Vienna is a very livable city, with a well-developed subway, train, tram and bus network and many supermarkets and pharmacies, and especially in spring I often saw very beautiful scenery. There were many people enjoying leisure time after work and relaxing on terrace seats, and it was a city rich in cultural activities such as orchestras and in history.

This study abroad was possible thanks to the support of a great many people and careful preparation. I was looked after by various people, such as the professors of the International Collaboration Office, the Frontier Association, my parents, friends and the doctors I met on site, and while overcoming small troubles and making many happy memories, I was able to finish my study abroad safely and come home. Thanks to everyone's support I was able to have such a valuable experience while still a student, and I sincerely thank them for letting me learn so much in terms of study, daily life and interaction.
